newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi says sees key interest rates falling.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says sees key interest rates falling.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said in an interview published on Monday that he foresaw a drop in key interest rates and that Italy's economic recovery was just around the corner.

"I think that in the space of a few weeks the turnaround will become really evident," he told Turin's La Stampa in an interview coinciding with Sunday's first anniversary of the swearing in of his centre-left government.
Prodi listed the accomplishments of his government's economic policy.
These included a halving of the public debt, leading Italy back into the European exchange rate mechanism, and a stop in the rise in the rate of unemployment.
"The discount rate, that is, the cost of money, has been reduced in a significant way and I foresee that (rates) will be reduced further," he said.

The central bank's discount rate stood at 9.0 pct when the centre-left government took office a year ago. It now stands at 6.75 and many analysts see another rate cut coming because of the steady slowdown in inflation.
Prodi said last week interest rates had not fallen as much as he would have liked.

Financial market expectations of further cut in the Bank of Italy's key discount rate have risen since inflation figures for April showed a year-on-year rate for the consumer price index of 1.7 percent.
This was down from 2.2 percent in March and 4.5 percent in April of 1996, the month before Prodi took office.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio has used declining inflation in the past to cut the rate.
This time, however, many analysts believe Fazio is awaiting details of the government's three-year economic programme, due out later this month, and the outcome of French elections.

A fall in official rates triggers lower bank rates, thus helping industry, and allows the government to reduce the costs of servicing Italy's huge public debt, improving its chances of cutting the public deficit.
